Order
or'der
n. and v. (regular arrangement, rank, succession; to arrange; rendering Hebrew arak and dibrah, Greek taxis)
From the Latin ordo, a row or rank, a term first of weaving and then of the army. Hebrew arak is to arrange or set in rows — used of laying wood on the altar and of drawing up a battle line — and Greek taxis is a military rank or fixed arrangement.

Biblical Definition

Order is regular arrangement, and Scripture presents it as a reflection of God's own character rather than a matter of taste. Paul grounds it there explicitly: God is not the author of confusion, and therefore “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40) — the closing rule of a chapter governing the conduct of public worship, which is why the regulative principle is a matter of obedience and not preference. Order in the church is also structural. Titus was left in Crete “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Titus 1:5), so that a congregation without properly ordained elders is, in the apostle's judgment, still lacking something. Paul commends the Colossians for it as a spiritual grace, “joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ” (Colossians 2:5), setting order beside steadfastness as things a pastor rejoices to see. The word also names a priestly succession: Christ is “a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4), a priesthood not by Levitical descent but by divine oath, and Hebrews builds its central argument on that phrase.

Webster 1828 Definition

Regular arrangement, rank, and succession. Because God is not the author of confusion, order in worship and in church government is obedience; and Christ is a priest after the order of Melchizedek.

expand to see more

ORDER, n. [L. ordo.] Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; a word of extensive application.

2. Proper state; as, the house is in order.

3. Rank; class; degree; also, a rule or regulation; a command.

4. Regular government or discipline; as, order in the church.

5. In Scripture, let all things be done decently and in order, 1 Cor. 14; a priest after the order of Melchizedek, Psa. 110.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 14:40 — "Let all things be done decently and in order."

Titus 1:5 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:"

Colossians 2:5 — "For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ."

Psalm 110:4 — "The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek."

Modern Corruption

Order is heard as constraint — the enemy of authenticity and of the Spirit's freedom. Scripture derives order from the character of God himself and makes it the condition, not the rival, of true liberty.

expand to see more

The spontaneity objection appears wherever structured worship is thought to quench the Spirit, and 1 Corinthians 14 is the decisive answer, because it is the chapter most concerned with the extraordinary gifts and it ends by commanding order. Paul's reason is theological rather than practical: God is not the author of confusion but of peace, so disorder in worship misrepresents God. A congregation that prizes unpredictability above the commanded elements has not become more spiritual; it has become less like the God it gathers to worship.

A second pressure is on church government. Titus 1:5 treats the ordination of elders as part of setting in order what is wanting, which is not compatible with treating polity as adiaphora to be arranged by preference or efficiency. The New Testament pattern is a plurality of elders and deacons in each local congregation. The principle to recover is that order is not the opposite of life — it is the shape life takes when it comes from a God of peace, and Paul rejoiced to behold it as gladly as he rejoiced to behold faith.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew arak is to arrange in rows, used of altar wood and of battle lines; dibrah is manner or order, the term in Psalm 110:4. Greek taxis is fixed arrangement or rank, and euschemonos means decently, becomingly.

expand to see more

Hebrew arak (H6186) — to set in order, to arrange in rows; used of the wood upon the altar.

Hebrew dibrah (H1700) — manner, order, cause; after the order of Melchizedek.

Hebrew maarakah (H4634) — a row, an army in battle array; order as a martial figure.

Greek taxis (G5010) — fixed arrangement, rank, order; used of both church order and Melchizedek's priesthood.

Greek euschemonos (G2156) — decently, in a becoming manner; joined to taxis in 1 Corinthians 14:40.

Usage

"Of the rule closing the chapter on public worship: let all things be done decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40)."

"Of church government still wanting until elders are ordained: set in order the things that are wanting (Titus 1:5)."

"Of Christ's priestly succession: a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4)."
